# SignalLab demonstration transcript

Duration: approximately 2 minutes 55 seconds. Actual application screenshots, edited with synthetic English narration. This is a guided demonstration, not continuous screen recording or learner-study footage.

## 0:00 — TK2233 Cybersecurity × HCI

SignalLab connects phishing decisions with security interface design. The difficult concept is balancing protection with interruption. This demonstration uses actual screenshots of the working public simulator, with synthetic narration. The messages and scores are fictional teaching examples.

## 0:19 — Predict first · Threshold 4

Before seeing the results, learners predict what lowering a warning threshold will do. At threshold four, the same eight messages produce three threats warned, one threat missed, one unnecessary interruption, and three routine tasks allowed. These are calculated outcomes.

## 0:38 — Change the input · Threshold 2

Lowering the threshold to two catches all four authored threats, while interrupting two legitimate tasks. The messages have not changed. The warning rule has changed. This makes the trade-off visible instead of suggesting that more warnings automatically solve every problem.

## 0:56 — Open the calculation · P3 at threshold 4

The selected message has three points for an unfamiliar service and one for urgency. Four is at least four, so the rule shows a warning. Mira explains the process. The supplied phishing label determines the outcome category; the score does not prove legitimacy.

## 1:14 — Compare interfaces · Minimal warning

The design lab holds message evidence fixed while the warning presentation changes. The minimal condition gives less specific support. Learners can inspect the sender and destination. These interface variants demonstrate design choices; they do not predict how real people will respond.

## 1:32 — Compare interfaces · Actionable guidance

Actionable guidance explains relevant evidence and offers a concrete next step. This connects visibility and error prevention to cybersecurity decisions. In guided practice, cautious verification remains a safe alternative. Difficulty guidance suggests more support after two consecutive risky decisions.

## 1:53 — Apply the principle · Fresh cases

The transfer check asks for both an action and a reason in three new situations. Teaching explanations wait until the complete set is submitted. Confidence is recorded separately. This is a short learning exercise, and its results do not establish real-world detection ability.

## 2:12 — Recall and reflect · Local learning record

The report distinguishes first decisions from repeated practice. Recall questions hide the inbox and ask learners to retrieve the principles. Previously missed recall items return on reopening. Progress stays in the browser, and an export can preserve the actual practice record.

## 2:30 — Research, checks and remaining human review

Scopus AI and NotebookLM helped examine research, alongside the NIST guide and warning studies. The public repository records AI corrections, calculation tests and limitations. Real classmate trials, course-note alignment and optional lecturer review remain pending. This video presents software behavior, not measured learning gains.
